Image Processing · Lab 13 · Material

Aligned Images and Annotations

MaterialPracticeQuiz

Keep every label attached to the pixels it describes. You will transform a parcel image, its mask, its box and an arrow-tip keypoint as one consistent record.

What you will learn

  • Distinguish pixel-edge box coordinates from pixel-center keypoints.
  • Apply the same sampled geometry to images and annotations.
  • Use nearest interpolation and a separate ignore label for masks.
  • Clip boxes, flag invisible keypoints and audit alignment.

Before this lab: Use affine matrices, array slicing, nearest interpolation and seeded augmentation.

In this lab

  1. Annotation Coordinate Contracts
  2. Shared Horizontal Reflection
  3. Translation and Ignore Padding
  4. Cropping and Visibility
  5. Letterboxing with Rounded Dimensions
  6. Rotated Boxes and All Four Corners
  7. Photometric Changes Leave Geometry Alone
  8. Alignment Fault Diagnosis

Prepare your notebook

Use a Python notebook with OpenCV, Pillow, NumPy and Matplotlib. Run the setup once, then run the guided blocks in order. The copy button selects only the code.

The examples were checked with OpenCV 4.13, Pillow 12.3, NumPy 2.2 and Matplotlib 3.11. The repository’s Python requirements list the versions. These pages and images open offline; running the code requires the Python libraries.

Mask IDs: 0=table, 1=parcel, 255=ignore. Boxes use [x1,y1,x2,y2] continuous pixel edges; points use (x,y) pixel centers indexed from zero. Visible center coordinates use the inclusive grid domain 0..W−1 and 0..H−1.

Python · shared setup
import json
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from io import BytesIO
import numpy as np
import cv2
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
cv2.setNumThreads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(213)

# Drawn tabletop fixtures: RGB uint8, H=128, W=160, C=3.
def scene(kind="mug", seed=0):
    local = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:128, :160]
    grain = 4 * np.sin(xx / 3) + local.normal(0, 1, (128, 160))
    base = np.stack([205 + yy / 8 + grain, 191 + yy / 10 + grain,
                     166 + yy / 12 + grain], axis=-1)
    canvas = Image.fromarray(np.clip(base, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8))
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(canvas)
    for y in range(12, 128, 24):
        draw.line((0, y, 159, y), fill=(184, 168, 146), width=1)
    if kind == "mug":
        draw.ellipse((105, 43, 139, 87), fill=(53, 118, 167))
        draw.ellipse((112, 50, 131, 80), fill=(208, 193, 168))
        draw.rounded_rectangle((43, 33, 115, 102), radius=12, fill=(66, 145, 194))
        draw.ellipse((43, 27, 115, 48), fill=(34, 71, 91))
        draw.ellipse((48, 31, 110, 43), fill=(116, 71, 40))
        draw.text((64, 64), "TEA", fill=(245, 246, 237))
    elif kind == "parcel":
        draw.rectangle((27, 31, 123, 101), fill=(174, 117, 65), outline=(70, 45, 28), width=2)
        draw.rectangle((69, 32, 80, 100), fill=(224, 190, 124))
        draw.rectangle((86, 48, 115, 77), fill=(247, 244, 225))
        draw.text((89, 55), "UP", fill=(25, 30, 34))
        draw.line((39, 64, 39, 45), fill=(25, 30, 34), width=3)
        draw.polygon([(33, 48), (45, 48), (39, 41)], fill=(25, 30, 34))
    elif kind == "apple":
        draw.ellipse((43, 38, 115, 108), fill=(190, 48, 40))
        draw.ellipse((58, 44, 75, 63), fill=(241, 123, 93))
        draw.line((80, 42, 86, 26), fill=(75, 63, 32), width=5)
        draw.ellipse((84, 25, 104, 35), fill=(54, 117, 56))
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unknown fixture kind")
    return np.asarray(canvas).copy()

def panels(images, titles, cmap=None):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(images), figsize=(4 * len(images), 3.4), squeeze=False)
    for ax, image, title in zip(axes[0], images, titles):
        ax.imshow(image, cmap=cmap)
        ax.set_title(title)
        ax.axis("off")
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap

# One parcel occupies this exact pixel rectangle; class 0=table, 1=parcel.
def annotated_parcel():
    image = scene("parcel")
    mask = np.zeros((128, 160), np.uint8)
    mask[31:102, 27:124] = 1
    boxes = np.array([[27., 31., 124., 102.]])
    points = np.array([[39., 41.]])  # Arrow tip: discrete pixel-center coordinates.
    return image, mask, boxes, points

# Display boxes in edge coordinates; display center-coordinate points at +0.5.
def annotation_panels(records, titles):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, len(records), figsize=(4.3*len(records), 6), squeeze=False)
    colors = ListedColormap(["#e7dec9", "#cc914b", "#8b4cc9"])
    for col, ((image, mask, boxes, points), title) in enumerate(zip(records, titles)):
        h, w = image.shape[:2]
        axes[0,col].imshow(image, extent=(0,w,h,0))
        for x1,y1,x2,y2 in boxes:
            axes[0,col].add_patch(Rectangle((x1,y1),x2-x1,y2-y1,fill=False,edgecolor="#00ffff",linewidth=2))
        if len(points):
            axes[0,col].scatter(points[:,0]+0.5,points[:,1]+0.5,c="#ff00ff",s=35)
        display_mask = np.where(mask==255,2,mask)
        axes[1,col].imshow(display_mask,cmap=colors,vmin=0,vmax=2,extent=(0,w,h,0),interpolation="nearest")
        axes[0,col].set_title(title)
        axes[1,col].set_title("Mask: table / parcel / ignore\ncream / brown / purple",fontsize=10)
        for ax in axes[:,col]:
            ax.set_xlim(0,w)
            ax.set_ylim(h,0)
            ax.axis("off")
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

The image comparisons below come from the guided code. Use their captions and shared display scales to compare each change.

Guided task 01

Annotation Coordinate Contracts

An image array uses row, column, channel order, but geometric coordinates are written (x,y), meaning column then row. Our rectangular parcel occupies rows 31 through 101 and columns 27 through 123. Its continuous pixel-edge box is [27,31,124,102]: the upper bounds lie just beyond the last included pixels. Box width is x2−x1, with no added one under this convention.

The arrow-tip keypoint is different. Point (39,41) names the center of that indexed pixel, so horizontal reflection later uses W−1−x. A plot displayed with extent (0,W,H,0) places that center at (39.5,41.5); the display helper adds the half pixel, but the stored annotation remains unchanged. Write these conventions down before combining libraries. A one-pixel discrepancy can be a convention mismatch rather than a random numerical error.

Try it

  1. Create the image, mask, box and arrow-tip point.
  2. Compute box width, height and mask area.
  3. Inspect the shared overlay and the categorical mask.
Python · run in order
image, mask, boxes, points = annotated_parcel()
box_width = boxes[0,2] - boxes[0,0]
box_height = boxes[0,3] - boxes[0,1]
mask_area = int(np.count_nonzero(mask == 1))
fig = annotation_panels([(image,mask,boxes,points)], ["Original annotated parcel"])

Read the result

The cyan box encloses exactly the parcel's pixel rectangle and the magenta point marks the arrow tip. Purple is reserved for ignored pixels and is absent from this original fixture. The box describes extent, not the parcel's internal tape or text.

Change and compare

  • Convert one box edge to its adjacent pixel index explicitly.
  • Compare box area with the count of parcel-mask pixels.

Guided task 02

Shared Horizontal Reflection

Reflection is a useful first alignment test because it can be exact and requires no interpolation. Reverse columns in both RGB and mask arrays. For continuous box edges, the reflected interval is [W−x2, W−x1], preserving the ordering of the left and right edges. For a pixel-center keypoint, use W−1−x. The difference of one is deliberate, not a correction to add indiscriminately.

Copy every annotation before changing it so the raw record remains available for comparison. The printed parcel text becomes mirrored, making this operation appropriate only for a task whose target permits it. Here we are practicing parcel location and arrow-tip location rather than reading the word or classifying its direction. Coordinate consistency cannot rescue a policy that violates the target definition, so both semantic and geometric checks are required.

Try it

  1. Reverse columns in RGB and mask together.
  2. Reflect box edges and point centers using their own formulas.
  3. Verify that applying reflection twice recovers the record.
Python · run in order
h,w = image.shape[:2]
flip_image = image[:,::-1].copy()
flip_mask = mask[:,::-1].copy()
flip_boxes = boxes.copy()
flip_boxes[:,0] = w - boxes[:,2]
flip_boxes[:,2] = w - boxes[:,0]
flip_points = points.copy()
flip_points[:,0] = w - 1 - points[:,0]
fig = annotation_panels([(image,mask,boxes,points),(flip_image,flip_mask,flip_boxes,flip_points)], ["Original", "Aligned reflection"])

Read the result

The arrow-tip point travels with the arrow while the box width remains unchanged. A point formula applied to box edges would introduce a systematic offset even though the transformed picture itself looked correct.

Change and compare

  • Apply the reflection formulas again and compare with all original annotations.
  • Explain why a text-reading label would require a different policy.

Guided task 03

Translation and Ignore Padding

Use a single forward translation matrix for RGB and mask. RGB can use linear interpolation, while categorical masks require nearest-neighbor sampling so a class ID is never blended with another ID. Padding has no observed source label. We therefore reserve 255 as ignore, separate from class 0, which explicitly means table. A future loss or metric must be configured to exclude ignored positions.

Move the parcel 42 pixels right and 7 down. Its right edge passes outside the canvas, so translate the box and clip its edges to the output extent. The keypoint stays visible in this example. An annotation box outside the image is not fixed by changing the picture alone. Inspect the purple padding band and the clipped cyan box together: they represent different effects, missing source coverage and a partially cropped object.

Try it

  1. Translate RGB and mask with the same matrix.
  2. Pad mask with ignore ID 255.
  3. Translate and clip the box to width 160 and height 128.
Python · run in order
dx,dy = 42,7
transform = np.float32([[1,0,dx],[0,1,dy]])
shift_image = cv2.warpAffine(image,transform,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderValue=(225,218,200))
shift_mask = cv2.warpAffine(mask,transform,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST,borderValue=255)
shift_boxes = boxes + np.array([dx,dy,dx,dy])
shift_boxes[:,[0,2]] = np.clip(shift_boxes[:,[0,2]],0,w)
shift_boxes[:,[1,3]] = np.clip(shift_boxes[:,[1,3]],0,h)
shift_points = points + np.array([dx,dy])
fig = annotation_panels([(image,mask,boxes,points),(shift_image,shift_mask,shift_boxes,shift_points)], ["Original", "Translated and clipped"])

Read the result

Ignore padding does not mean background, and the clipped box does not claim that the full parcel remains visible. Nearest interpolation keeps the legal label vocabulary even where RGB interpolation mixes neighboring colors.

Change and compare

  • Translate left enough to move the arrow point outside and flag it invisible.
  • Replace mask padding with 0 only as a diagnostic and describe the false supervision it would create.

Guided task 04

Cropping and Visibility

A crop changes the coordinate origin. Subtract its left offset from every x coordinate and its top offset from every y coordinate, then clip box edges to the crop extent. Drop boxes with zero width or height after clipping, and use the same keep flags to filter class IDs. The parcel remains partly visible in our crop, but the arrow-tip point does not. Do not clamp an invisible point onto the nearest border: that would invent a new location for a feature that is absent.

A visibility flag retains the distinction between a stored coordinate and a usable target. Our visibility policy uses the inclusive domain between the first and last pixel centers, including for fractional transformed coordinates. We keep the transformed point value and display it only if 0≤x≤W−1 and 0≤y≤H−1. Box retention is measured as the clipped box area divided by its original area before cropping. This ratio describes rectangular extent, not true object-pixel visibility for an arbitrary shape. A dataset policy must state its retention threshold and what happens to dropped annotations.

Try it

  1. Crop rows 10:110 and columns 65:155.
  2. Subtract the crop origin from boxes and points.
  3. Measure box retention and flag the point's visibility.
Python · run in order
top,left,ch,cw = 10,65,100,90
crop_image = image[top:top+ch,left:left+cw]
crop_mask = mask[top:top+ch,left:left+cw]
def clip_and_keep(input_boxes,width,height):
    clipped = input_boxes.copy()
    clipped[:,[0,2]] = np.clip(clipped[:,[0,2]],0,width)
    clipped[:,[1,3]] = np.clip(clipped[:,[1,3]],0,height)
    keep = (clipped[:,2]>clipped[:,0]) & (clipped[:,3]>clipped[:,1])
    return clipped[keep],keep
crop_raw_boxes = boxes - np.array([left,top,left,top])
box_classes = np.array([1],dtype=np.int64)
crop_boxes,box_keep = clip_and_keep(crop_raw_boxes,cw,ch)
crop_box_classes = box_classes[box_keep]
crop_points = points - np.array([left,top])
def visible_centers(point_array,width,height):
    return (point_array[:,0]>=0)&(point_array[:,0]<=width-1)&(point_array[:,1]>=0)&(point_array[:,1]<=height-1)
visible = visible_centers(crop_points,cw,ch)
retention = ((crop_boxes[:,2]-crop_boxes[:,0])*(crop_boxes[:,3]-crop_boxes[:,1])) / ((boxes[box_keep,2]-boxes[box_keep,0])*(boxes[box_keep,3]-boxes[box_keep,1]))
fig = annotation_panels([(image,mask,boxes,points),(crop_image,crop_mask,crop_boxes,crop_points[visible])], ["Original", f"Crop; box retention {retention[0]:.2f}"])

Read the result

The absence of a displayed magenta point is an intentional visibility result, not an omitted transform. The remaining box touches the crop's left edge because part of the parcel was removed there.

Change and compare

  • Choose a crop that retains the arrow and compare the visibility flag.
  • Use a 0.7 retention rule to decide whether this box would be kept.

Guided task 05

Letterboxing with Rounded Dimensions

Letterboxing resizes while approximately preserving aspect ratio and then pads to a fixed canvas. A requested common scale is not enough for annotation math because the resized dimensions are integers. For a 192-by-192 canvas, the width becomes 192 and the rounded height becomes 154. Use actual scales sx=192/160 and sy=154/128 rather than assuming they are exactly equal.

Continuous box edges scale directly and then receive the padding offset. Pixel-center coordinates follow the resize center mapping: (x+0.5)×sx−0.5, followed by the offset. This half-pixel form describes the geometric location; discrete nearest mask boundaries may differ by a sampled pixel. Resize RGB with linear interpolation for enlargement, resize the mask with nearest, and fill mask padding with ignore. Store actual dimensions and padding so this transformation can be replayed and inspected.

Try it

  1. Round the resized height for a 192-square canvas.
  2. Compute scales from actual dimensions.
  3. Resize and pad all annotations under their conventions.
Python · run in order
out_w,out_h = 192,192
scale = min(out_w/w,out_h/h)
new_w,new_h = round(w*scale),round(h*scale)
sx,sy = new_w/w,new_h/h
pad_x,pad_y = (out_w-new_w)//2,(out_h-new_h)//2
letter_image = np.full((out_h,out_w,3),(225,218,200),np.uint8)
letter_mask = np.full((out_h,out_w),255,np.uint8)
letter_image[pad_y:pad_y+new_h,pad_x:pad_x+new_w] = cv2.resize(image,(new_w,new_h),interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
letter_mask[pad_y:pad_y+new_h,pad_x:pad_x+new_w] = cv2.resize(mask,(new_w,new_h),interpolation=cv2.INTER_NEAREST)
letter_boxes = boxes * np.array([sx,sy,sx,sy]) + np.array([pad_x,pad_y,pad_x,pad_y])
letter_points = (points+0.5)*np.array([sx,sy])-0.5+np.array([pad_x,pad_y])
fig = annotation_panels([(image,mask,boxes,points),(letter_image,letter_mask,letter_boxes,letter_points)], ["Original", "192-square letterbox"])

Read the result

The purple horizontal bands are ignored padding, not table labels. The two actual scale factors differ slightly because height was rounded; using the requested scale everywhere would silently introduce annotation drift.

Change and compare

  • Compute the point using scale alone and measure the vertical discrepancy.
  • Repeat on a 181-square canvas and record unequal top and bottom padding if it occurs.

Guided task 06

Rotated Boxes and All Four Corners

After rotation, transforming only the top-left and bottom-right corners is insufficient: another corner may supply a new minimum or maximum. Transform all four box corners, take their x and y extrema, and clip the enclosing axis-aligned box to the output extent. That enclosing rectangle can include background even when the original box was tight. It is a geometric enclosure, not a segmentation mask.

OpenCV's rotation matrix acts on indexed pixel-center coordinates. Our box corners use edge coordinates, whose origin is half a pixel away. Convert an edge point to center coordinates by subtracting 0.5, apply the matrix, then add 0.5 back. The code expresses that change as a homogeneous matrix conjugation. Keypoints use the original center-coordinate matrix directly. Keeping both matrices explicitly named prevents an attractive overlay from hiding a convention mismatch.

Try it

  1. Build a 14-degree center-coordinate affine matrix.
  2. Convert it to the edge-coordinate convention.
  3. Transform all four box corners and the arrow-tip point.
Python · run in order
center_matrix = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(((w-1)/2,(h-1)/2),14,1.0)
homogeneous = np.vstack([center_matrix,[0,0,1]])
to_centers = np.array([[1,0,-.5],[0,1,-.5],[0,0,1]])
to_edges = np.array([[1,0,.5],[0,1,.5],[0,0,1]])
edge_matrix = to_edges @ homogeneous @ to_centers
x1,y1,x2,y2 = boxes[0]
corners = np.array([[x1,y1,1],[x2,y1,1],[x2,y2,1],[x1,y2,1]])
moved_corners = corners @ edge_matrix.T
rot_box = np.array([[moved_corners[:,0].min(),moved_corners[:,1].min(),moved_corners[:,0].max(),moved_corners[:,1].max()]])
rot_box[:,[0,2]] = np.clip(rot_box[:,[0,2]],0,w)
rot_box[:,[1,3]] = np.clip(rot_box[:,[1,3]],0,h)
rot_points = np.column_stack([points,np.ones(len(points))]) @ center_matrix.T
rot_image = cv2.warpAffine(image,center_matrix,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderValue=(225,218,200))
rot_mask = cv2.warpAffine(mask,center_matrix,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST,borderValue=255)
fig = annotation_panels([(image,mask,boxes,points),(rot_image,rot_mask,rot_box,rot_points)], ["Original", "Rotation with enclosing box"])

Read the result

The cyan rectangle grows around the tilted parcel. Its unused corner regions are expected, whereas a box that cuts through the parcel would indicate an incorrect coordinate calculation or inappropriate clipping.

Change and compare

  • Compare all-corner bounds with bounds from only two opposite corners.
  • Set the angle to zero and verify both coordinate conventions return the original annotations.

Guided task 07

Photometric Changes Leave Geometry Alone

Not every augmentation belongs on every field. A brightness offset changes RGB values but does not move pixels. Applying that same arithmetic to a categorical mask would corrupt class IDs; applying it to a box would move annotations without moving the object. The correct shared-record policy identifies which operations affect geometry and which affect appearance.

Use a modest −25 offset on the reflected RGB image while copying its mask, box and keypoint unchanged. This sequence composes an earlier geometric change with a new photometric one. The mask remains a target description, not a grayscale image to be enhanced. Check exact annotation equality after the appearance step. If an appearance operation makes the object invisible, the geometry can still be numerically aligned while the training example becomes semantically unusable.

Try it

  1. Start from the already reflected record.
  2. Change only the RGB image's brightness.
  3. Compare unchanged annotations before and after.
Python · run in order
dim_image = np.rint(np.clip(flip_image.astype(np.float32)-25,0,255)).astype(np.uint8)
dim_mask = flip_mask.copy()
dim_boxes = flip_boxes.copy()
dim_points = flip_points.copy()
fig = annotation_panels([(flip_image,flip_mask,flip_boxes,flip_points),(dim_image,dim_mask,dim_boxes,dim_points)], ["Reflected record", "Brightness only"])

Read the result

The cyan extent, magenta point and mask boundaries stay fixed while the image darkens. A good pipeline does not blindly run an image transform over all arrays that happen to be stored in the same record.

Change and compare

  • Verify that the legal mask IDs remain exactly the same.
  • Propose which fields a JPEG round trip should affect and which it should leave untouched.

Guided task 08

Alignment Fault Diagnosis

A shared seed is not a substitute for shared parameters. If an image and its mask independently request values from a generator, they can receive different displacements. A simpler but equally damaging bug is transforming the image and forgetting the mask entirely. Shapes and legal class IDs may still pass validation while supervision points to the wrong pixels.

Construct one correct integer translation and one deliberately stale-mask record. The expected mask is known because the geometry is exact; count disagreements only in the translated mask's non-ignored region. This is a pipeline correctness check, not a model accuracy measurement. In real datasets, overlays and known synthetic fixtures complement unit tests because no single generic shape assertion proves alignment. Keep a tiny, exact annotation fixture in the test suite when replacing libraries or changing coordinate conventions.

Try it

  1. Translate RGB and all coordinates by (8,−5).
  2. Generate the matching nearest-neighbor mask.
  3. Display a deliberately stale mask as a labeled fault.
Python · run in order
audit_matrix = np.float32([[1,0,8],[0,1,-5]])
audit_image = cv2.warpAffine(image,audit_matrix,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST,borderValue=(225,218,200))
audit_mask = cv2.warpAffine(mask,audit_matrix,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST,borderValue=255)
audit_boxes = boxes + [8,-5,8,-5]
audit_points = points + [8,-5]
valid_region = audit_mask != 255
stale_disagreements = int(np.count_nonzero((mask != audit_mask) & valid_region))
fig = annotation_panels([(audit_image,audit_mask,audit_boxes,audit_points),(audit_image,mask,audit_boxes,audit_points)], ["Correct shared translation", f"FAULT: stale mask ({stale_disagreements} mismatches)"])

Read the result

The fault panel has a plausible image, a legal mask and correct output dimensions. Its stale target is still wrong. Exact synthetic alignment tests expose this class of error before a future model is asked to learn from the data.

Change and compare

  • Repeat the diagnostic with a stale keypoint instead of a stale mask.
  • Use zero displacement and verify the stale-mask diagnostic no longer reports a difference.
